claims.text: Accelerated simultaneous wear-corrosion degradation in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys arises from galvanic cells associated with contiguous phase boundaries.
Mechanical wear exposes phase boundaries and disrupts the passive or oxide film.
Electrochemically dissimilar phases exposed at phase boundaries establish localized galvanic cells.
The localized galvanic cells accelerate selective dissolution and localized corrosion.
Wear-induced film rupture and galvanic corrosion act together to accelerate coupled degradation.
An as-cast CoCrFeMnNi eutectic high-entropy alloy can contain Mn-rich phases and contiguous, interconnected phase boundaries that promote galvanic interactions.
Thermomechanical processing involving hot rolling near 900°C, quenching, and possible cold deformation refines the microstructure.
The proposed thermomechanical processing partially disconnects phase interfaces and reduces their electrical connectivity.
Microstructural refinement disrupts continuous phase interfaces.
Reduced phase connectivity limits galvanic interactions.
Limiting galvanic interactions mitigates synergistic wear-corrosion degradation.
Refined samples will have significantly lower total degradation than matched as-cast samples.
Refined samples will have lower wear depths than matched as-cast samples.
Refined samples will have lower corrosion rates than matched as-cast samples.
The comparison should be conducted at 300–350°C in salt spray or molten salt under identical wear parameters.
Phase-boundary connectivity can be quantified by electron microscopy and image-based connectivity analysis.
Wear depth, corrosion current density, potential shifts, and electrochemical impedance parameters provide measurable responses for the controlled comparison.
Failure of refined samples to reduce both wear and corrosion rates would falsify phase connectivity as the primary degradation driver.
Finding similar phase connectivity in the processed and as-cast samples would falsify the proposed phase-connectivity mechanism.
